**Time allowed: three hours.** Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0, Al = 27.0, S = 32.0, Na = 23.0, Fe = 56.

The paper is arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry; Section B - Inorganic Chemistry; Section C - Organic Chemistry.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) How would you identify the presence of

(i) A double bond

(ii) Chlorine *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Double bond (C=C).** Shake the compound with **bromine water** (or a solution of bromine in an inert solvent) at room temperature: the **orange-brown colour is decolourised** (addition across $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ gives a colourless dibromo compound). Alternatively, add **cold dilute acidified (or alkaline) potassium manganate(VII)**: the **purple colour is decolourised** (or turns brown/green in alkaline solution) as the alkene is oxidised to a diol.

**(ii) Chlorine.** Use the **sodium fusion (Lassaigne) test**, which converts covalently bound chlorine into chloride ions: fuse a small sample with a piece of sodium, heat until red hot and plunge into distilled water; boil and filter. Acidify the filtrate with **dilute nitric acid** (to remove carbonate, sulphide and cyanide) and add **aqueous silver nitrate**: a **white precipitate of silver chloride**, soluble in dilute aqueous ammonia, shows that chlorine was present: $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)}$.

(For a chloroalkane an alternative is to warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide, acidify with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous silver nitrate; the vinylic chlorine of a chloroalkene is very resistant to this hydrolysis, which is why the fusion test is preferred.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) If 0.485 g of the compound, A, contains 0.120 g of carbon, 0.01 g of hydrogen, calculate the empirical formula of the compound. *[2 marks]*

(ii) 0.485 g of compound A reacted completely with 1.700 g of silver nitrate in the ratio 1:2. (Molar mass of silver nitrate is 170 g/mol). Determine

A. The molar mass of compound A

B. The molecular formula of compound A *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Empirical formula.** The compound contains only H, C and Cl (stated in the introduction), so the mass of chlorine is found by difference:

$m(\mathrm{Cl}) = 0.485 - 0.120 - 0.010 = 0.355\ \mathrm{g}$

| Element | Mass (g) | Moles = mass / RAM | Ratio (divide by 0.0100) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | 0.120 | $0.120 / 12.0 = 0.0100$ | 1 |
| H | 0.010 | $0.010 / 1.0 = 0.0100$ | 1 |
| Cl | 0.355 | $0.355 / 35.5 = 0.0100$ | 1 |

**Empirical formula: $\mathrm{CHCl}$** (empirical formula mass $12.0 + 1.0 + 35.5 = 48.5$).

**(ii) A. Molar mass.** $n(\mathrm{AgNO_3}) = \dfrac{1.700}{170} = 0.0100\ \mathrm{mol}$.

A reacts with $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ in the ratio $1 : 2$, so $n(\mathrm{A}) = \dfrac{0.0100}{2} = 0.00500\ \mathrm{mol}$.

$M(\mathrm{A}) = \dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{0.485}{0.00500} = 97\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

**B. Molecular formula.** $n = \dfrac{97}{48.5} = 2$, so the molecular formula is $2 \times \mathrm{CHCl} = $ **$\mathrm{C_2H_2Cl_2}$** (dichloroethene, $M = 24 + 2 + 71 = 97$).

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) Give two isomers of compound A *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Compound A is $\mathrm{C_2H_2Cl_2}$ (dichloroethene), which has a double bond. Two of its isomers:

1. **1,1-dichloroethene**, $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CCl_2}$ (positional isomer: both chlorine atoms on the same carbon);
2. **cis-1,2-dichloroethene** (Z), $\mathrm{ClHC{=}CHCl}$ with the two Cl atoms on the same side of the double bond.

(The third isomer is **trans-1,2-dichloroethene** (E), with the two Cl atoms on opposite sides. Cis and trans are geometric isomers because rotation about $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ is restricted.)

(d) (i) Complete the table below by giving the structure and name of a primary, secondary and tertiary amine with molecular formula $\mathrm{C_3H_9N}$

| Class | Structure | Name |
|---|---|---|
| 1° | | |
| 2° | | |
| 3° | | |

(ii) Primary amines can be prepared from amides by Hoffmann's degradation.

(a) Write a general equation for the reaction.

(b) Give reagents and reaction conditions for the reaction.

(iii) What feature of amines is responsible for their being basic?

(iv) Suggest one way of increasing the basicity of an amine. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Isomers of $\mathrm{C_3H_9N}$.**

| Class | Structure | Name |
|---|---|---|
| 1° | $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}$ (or $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHNH_2}$) | propylamine, propan-1-amine (or propan-2-amine) |
| 2° | $\mathrm{CH_3NHCH_2CH_3}$ | N-methylethanamine (ethylmethylamine) |
| 3° | $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}$ | N,N-dimethylmethanamine (trimethylamine) |

A primary amine has one alkyl group on N ($\mathrm{R{-}NH_2}$), a secondary amine two ($\mathrm{R_2NH}$), a tertiary amine three ($\mathrm{R_3N}$).

**(ii) Hofmann degradation** (the product has one carbon fewer than the amide).

(a) General equation: $\mathrm{RCONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{RNH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$

(b) Reagents and conditions: **bromine and concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide** (or potassium hydroxide, or sodium hypobromite formed in situ), **warmed** gently (about $50\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $70\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

**(iii)** The amines are basic because of the **lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom**, which can accept a proton (Bronsted-Lowry base) or be donated to form a dative bond (Lewis base): $\mathrm{RNH_2} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{RNH_3^+}$.

**(iv) Increasing the basicity.** Attach **electron-releasing (electron-donating) alkyl groups** to the nitrogen atom (for example replace a hydrogen of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ by an alkyl group, or use a larger alkyl group). Their positive inductive effect ($+I$) increases the electron density on N, so the lone pair holds a proton more readily (for example $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$ is a stronger base than $\mathrm{NH_3}$). Electron-withdrawing groups (such as a phenyl ring, as in phenylamine) have the opposite effect.
